issues.legal_issue: A court may use its inherent power to recall an order permitting withdrawal of a suit when the withdrawal was sought by someone who lacked authority to act for the plaintiff and the court was misled about that authority.
material_facts: A society brought a suit concerning immovable property through its then Secretary.
Another person later claimed to be the society’s Secretary and sought withdrawal of the suit; the application was allowed without notice to the then Secretary or the lawyers who had brought the suit.
A later Secretary applied to recall the withdrawal order and restore the suit, alleging that the person who sought withdrawal had not been elected and lacked authority.
The trial court rejected the recall application as not maintainable and found that the person who sought withdrawal had been elected Secretary.
The High Court acknowledged serious errors in the trial court’s determination of who was Secretary but declined to correct them, reasoning that it lacked jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court held that the authority question required reconsideration and did not itself finally determine who had been elected Secretary.
issues.conclusion: The application to recall the withdrawal order was maintainable. If the applicant’s account is established—that the person seeking withdrawal lacked authority—the withdrawal request was not made for the plaintiff, the court was misled, and the order must be vacated. The matter was remitted for reconsideration.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a court has inherent power to correct its proceedings when a party has misled it into making an order. That principle applies when a suit is withdrawn on a request purportedly made for the plaintiff by an unauthorized person. The court may investigate whether consent was in fact given where the court was misled by a representation that consent existed; a claim that consent was procured by fraud, where the party was in fact a party to the compromise, must instead be pursued by suit. The Court approved Sadho Saran Rai v. Anant Rai, Vilakathala Raman v. Vayalil Pachu, and Basangowda Hanmantgowda Patil v. Churchugirigowda Yogangowda.

predicates.recall_application_after_suit_withdrawal: A plaintiff or someone acting for the plaintiff applies to recall an order that permitted the suit to be withdrawn.
predicates.purported_representative_lacked_authorit: The person who sought withdrawal was not authorized to act for the plaintiff.
predicates.court_misled_by_authority_claim: The court permitted withdrawal because it was led to believe that the person seeking it was authorized to act for the plaintiff.

issues.definition: When an unauthorized person obtains withdrawal of a suit by misleading the court about their authority, the court may recall the withdrawal order.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may exercise revisional jurisdiction when a trial court fails to exercise jurisdiction vested in it by refusing to consider an application invoking its inherent power.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the application to recall the withdrawal order as not maintainable and proceeded to decide who had been elected Secretary.
The High Court recognized that the trial court had made serious errors in deciding the Secretary’s election but declined to correct them on the assumption that it lacked jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court held that the trial court had failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in it and that the High Court should have intervened.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have exercised its revisional power because the trial court had failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in it by law. The judgments below were set aside and the matter was remitted to the trial court for reconsideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits revisional intervention where a subordinate court has failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in it. The trial court’s refusal to entertain the application under section 151 was such a failure, and the High Court should have corrected it.

predicates.revision_proceeding: A party challenges a subordinate court’s order in a revisional proceeding.
predicates.trial_court_refused_to_exercise_jurisdic: The subordinate court declined to consider an application that fell within jurisdiction vested in it.

issues.definition: In a revision proceeding, when the subordinate court has declined to exercise jurisdiction vested in it, the High Court must intervene.
